title: Cerebellar Error Signals

html:
Having framed the cerebellar objective as predictive calibration, the physical question is how a microzone actually implements a predict–compare loop: which signals carry the prediction, which carry the error, where the comparison happens, and what makes it temporally precise. The answer is unusually clean, because the cerebellar cortex funnels two anatomically and physiologically distinct input streams onto a single output neuron. The primary output cells of the cerebellar cortex, Purkinje cells (1̃5 million), make kinematic predictions about ongoing movements via high-frequency simple spikes, and encode sensory error information about that movement in low-frequency complex spikes 1. The first stream is the mossy-fiber (2̃00 million) →\rightarrow granule-cell (4̃0 billion) →\rightarrow parallel-fiber pathway, which drives the Purkinje cell’s high-rate simple-spike discharge (typically tens of hertz) 2; the second is the climbing-fiber input from the inferior olive, which drives the sparse complex spike (1̃ Hz): a large, stereotyped burst whose occurrence is near-binary, thanks to the exceptionally reliable climbing-fiber synapse, but whose duration and spikelet count are graded in a way that scales the resulting plasticity 3. The working hypothesis of this subsection is therefore that the simple-spike stream carries the module’s running prediction while the complex-spike stream carries the teaching signal that reports when that prediction has failed 4, 5.

The logic of the loop follows directly from the objective established above. On each cycle a microzone emits a prediction through its Purkinje simple spikes; the world, or the rest of the nervous system, returns the actual consequence; a comparison somewhere in the circuit extracts the residual by which prediction and consequence disagree; that residual is delivered back to the same Purkinje cells as a sparse climbing-fiber teaching event; and the resulting plasticity adjusts the prediction so that the next cycle’s residual is smaller. What makes the cerebellar version of this loop unusually tractable to study is that its two limbs are carried by anatomically segregated pathways with opposite statistics — a dense, high-rate prediction stream and a sparse, low-rate error stream — that converge on one output cell whose plasticity binds them. The rest of this part develops this two-signal picture in four steps: the mossy-fiber/simple-spike pathway that carries the prediction; the climbing-fiber/complex-spike pathway that carries the error, together with the circuit that actually computes it; the mechanisms that make the whole loop temporally precise; and the question of whether this machinery is specific to movement or reused across the cerebellum’s non-motor territories.

Mossy fibers, granule cells, and simple spikes

The prediction limb begins with the mossy fibers, the cerebellum’s dominant afferent system, which collectively provide the information from which a forward model can estimate the consequences of an action: the state of the body and environment, the behavioral context, and motor-related signals indicating the action being generated 6, 7, 8. These variables are not carried in neatly segregated channels; individual mossy-fiber pathways can combine sensory, motor, and contextual information, while convergence within the granule-cell layer constructs high-dimensional, multimodal representations of the current task state 9, 10.

Mossy fibers arise from numerous precerebellar sources. The largest contingent comes through the pontine nuclei, which relay widespread cerebral-cortical activity—including motor preparation, sensory and association signals, goals, and higher-order behavioral context—into the granule-cell layer 11, 12, 6. Spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar pathways convey proprioceptive, cutaneous, and integrated spinal-circuit activity; importantly, some spinocerebellar signals reflect the state of spinal premotor networks and therefore function as internal copies of descending or spinally generated motor commands rather than as sensory feedback alone 7, 13. Vestibular afferents and vestibular nuclei provide information about head motion, orientation, and balance 14, 15. The lateral reticular nucleus integrates descending motor signals with sensory and premotor activity from spinal interneuronal circuits, supplying the cerebellum with a compound representation of the command being implemented and the bodily state in which it is implemented 16, 7.

Corollary-discharge or efference-copy information reaches the cerebellum through several task-dependent routes, including corticopontine pathways and collateral branches of descending brainstem and spinal motor systems 7, 6. Specialized pathways also provide efference-copy signals for particular control domains: for example, the nucleus prepositus participates principally in oculomotor and vestibular circuits and may convey internal signals related to eye and head movement, rather than serving as a general relay for all outgoing motor commands 17, 18. Thus, there is no single universal “efference-copy tract”; motor-command information is distributed across multiple mossy-fiber systems 7.

Mossy fibers also issue excitatory collaterals to the cerebellar nuclei, allowing related sensory, contextual, and motor-related input to reach both the cerebellar cortical microcircuit and its nuclear output stage 11, 19.

Heterogeneous mossy fiber input is then recoded by the granule cells. Each mossy fiber diverges onto hundreds of granule cells, and — contrary to the older assumption of unimodal relay — individual granule cells integrate mossy-fiber inputs from different sources, mixing, for example, basilar-pontine and proprioceptive streams onto the same cell 9. The result is the expansion recoding anticipated by Marr and Albus and formalized in modern kernel terms: the modest-dimensional mossy-fiber input is projected into an enormous, sparse granule-cell basis, from which a Purkinje cell can approximate a wide range of functions 20, 21, 22, 4. A mouse experiment images granule-cell and climbing-fiber activity (Figure) 74. Granule and climbing-fiber activity track reward timing (Figure).

The learned cortical output is carried by the Purkinje cell’s high-rate simple-spike discharge. Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and their simple spikes provide a continuous inhibitory signal–commonly tens of spikes per second and sometimes exceeding 100 Hz–to the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei 23, 24. In the simplified Marr–Albus picture, this discharge is the weighted readout of the parallel-fiber representation. Biophysically, however, it also reflects Purkinje cells’ intrinsic pacemaking, feedforward and lateral inhibition from molecular-layer interneurons, climbing-fiber interactions, and plasticity at several classes of synapse. It is therefore best described as the cerebellar cortex’s learned model-output stream, rather than as a literal linear readout of parallel-fiber weights alone.

Nor should the discharge of a single Purkinje cell necessarily be identified with the complete output of a cerebellar module. Neurons within deep cerebellar nuclei integrate convergent inhibition from populations of Purkinje cells with excitatory mossy-fiber and climbing-fiber collaterals; in many cases, the behaviorally relevant estimate or command becomes legible only after population-level convergence onto these downstream neurons 25, 26.

Several features make the simple-spike stream naturally interpretable as the output of a forward model. Its content is predictive: during movement, simple-spike firing encodes upcoming kinematics — position, velocity, and speed — with components that lead the movement rather than merely reporting it, and the timing distribution is biased toward prediction, with modulation on average preceding movement by roughly 100 ms 27, 28. This holds across effectors and tasks: the same predictive coding appears in vermal Purkinje cells during saccades and in intermediate/lateral-zone cells during manual tracking, which is what one would expect if the forward-model computation were a generic mode of cortical processing rather than a quirk of one motor system 29.

And this predictive code is legible at the population level in a form matched to control. In the oculomotor vermis, when Purkinje cells are grouped by their shared climbing-fiber input — that is, by complex-spike directional tuning — the combined simple-spike activity of the bursting and pausing cells predicts the real-time speed and direction of a saccade multiplicatively, as a gain field. Importantly, neither the bursting nor the pausing population alone suffices; the prediction is a property of the convergent input onto a cerebellar nucleus neuron, information no single cell carries 25. The prediction, in other words, is not an abstraction imposed by the modeller: it is present in the firing of the output cells, timed ahead of the movement, and organized by the very climbing-fiber map that will later teach it.

The label "prediction stream," however, requires immediate qualification, and this is the first place the two-signal picture becomes more subtle. Simple spikes do not encode predictions alone; they also encode the errors themselves. Individual Purkinje cells signal performance errors — how far the effector missed — independently of the kinematic signals they carry, and, strikingly, each variable (both kinematic and error) is represented twice: once by a component that leads the movement and once by a component that lags it, with a change in the sign of the modulation between the two 28, 30. A leading (predictive) and a lagging (feedback) copy of the same quantity is exactly what a neuron would carry if it were computing a sensory prediction error internally, by holding its own prediction against the feedback that arrives a moment later 5, 29. This matters for the architecture: part of the predict–compare operation is already visible in the cortical output, so the residual is not delivered exclusively by the separate error pathway described next. These paired signals span a wide temporal window — from tens of milliseconds to as much as two seconds around the movement in tracking tasks — consistent with a forward model that both anticipates consequences and retains a short memory of recent performance to inform the next action 30.

The classical error limb is carried by the climbing fibers, and its anatomy is as distinctive as its statistics. Every Purkinje cell in the adult cerebellum is innervated by single climbing fiber (with residual multi-innervation in some cells, perhaps more prominently in humans 31) from the inferior olive, a brainstem nucleus. That lone input forms one of the most powerful synapses in the nervous system: it wraps the soma and smooth proximal dendrite in anywhere from several hundred to over a thousand contact sites, each with high release probability, while the parallel fibers are confined to the spiny distal branchlets 32, 3. A single olivary spike therefore reliably drives a complex spike: a large calcium-based dendritic event consisting of an initial full spike followed by a brief burst of smaller spikelets, occurring at a low rate of roughly one per second against the Purkinje cell’s much faster simple-spike background 33, 34. In the Marr–Albus–Ito framework this sparse event is the instructive signal that guides plasticity, and recent causal work confirms the role directly: optogenetically supplied complex spikes are sufficient to serve as the teaching signal for associative cerebellar learning 35, 4. A monkey study compares pursuit learning and complex spikes (Figure). Recent human fMRI evidence extends cerebellar prediction-error signals to passive, nonmotor statistical learning (Figure). Model comparison distinguishes incremental cerebellar updating from hippocampal structure learning (Figure). Climbing-fiber stimulation can instruct eyeblink conditioning (Figure). Inferior-olive inhibition disrupts conditioned learning (Figure). The experiment measures complex-spike duration and probability (Figure).

For a teaching signal, though, the complex spike has a notorious problem: because the climbing-fiber synapse is so reliable, the postsynaptic response is nearly all-or-none within a given cell, which at first glance makes it a poor instrument for reporting the magnitude or sign of an error 33. The resolution is that the signal is graded at two levels the binary caricature misses. Within a cell, the complex spike is not truly invariant: the number of spikelets and the duration of the event vary with the size of the underlying olivary burst, and these variations are behaviourally consequential. Longer-duration complex spikes drive larger single-trial depression and stronger learning; a short climbing-fiber burst can bias plasticity toward potentiation while a longer burst drives depression, so the number of spikes even controls the direction of the change; and the dendritic calcium transient the complex spike delivers is itself graded during learning 36, 37, 38. Across cells, the olive grades the signal by which Purkinje cells it drives: each cell responds preferentially to errors in a particular direction — its "CS-on" direction — so a population of Purkinje cells within a microzone collectively encodes a directional error vector, and that vector in sensory space is aligned with the direction of the corrective force the module controls 1. Recent recordings extend this to reciprocally modulated parasagittal bands whose complex spiking encodes the sign and magnitude of an imposed perturbation 39. A near-binary event per cell thus becomes a graded, signed, directional teaching signal at the level of the microzone. A 2025 experiment tests climbing fibers during motor-memory acquisition (Figure) 75. The study also inhibits climbing fibers after acquisition (Figure).

None of this yet answers where the comparison — the actual subtraction of prediction from consequence — is performed. The classical picture places it implicitly at the Purkinje cell, but the decisive circuit element may lie at the other end of the loop, in the projection from the cerebellar nuclei back to the inferior olive. A subpopulation of small GABAergic nucleo-olivary neurons in the cerebellar nuclei projects to the olive, following the same zonal organization as the climbing fibers and thereby closing a reciprocal loop between olive, cortex, and nuclei 40, 41, 42. This inhibition delivers the cerebellum’s own output back to the source of its teaching signal, where it is subtracted from the incoming sensory error: if the module’s prediction matches the actual consequence, the two cancel and olivary activity stays at its baseline; only an unpredicted consequence drives the olive away from baseline and produces a climbing-fiber event 43, 44. This is the circuit-level implementation of two principles invoked in the loss section: the Rescorla–Wagner rule that learning occurs only when events violate expectation, and the adaptive-filter corollary that the cerebellum learns only when the olive is perturbed from baseline 43, 44. The consequences are directly demonstrable: a properly timed cerebello-olivary signal is by itself sufficient to drive extinction of a learned response, and omission of an expected outcome drives the olive precisely at the time the outcome was predicted 45. The comparison, in short, is distributed and recurrent: the cortex already carries paired prediction and feedback signals, while the nucleo-olivary loop performs an explicit subtraction that converts sensory error into a teaching-relevant prediction error before it ever reaches the Purkinje cell.

One caveat about the subtraction deserves stating, because it changes what kind of operation we should say the olive is performing. The account above treats the olive computationally as a subtraction node: prediction in, sensory error in, surprise out. Mechanistically, however, the inferior olive is not a simple monotonic firing-rate subtractor. Olivary neurons are electrically coupled through gap junctions concentrated between dendritic spines within the glomeruli (specialized synaptic structures), and many—but not all, and not necessarily continuously—exhibit prominent subthreshold membrane-potential oscillations. Nucleo-olivary inhibition can therefore do more than simply reduce firing probability: it can hyperpolarize the neuron, recruit rebound conductances, reset and alter the amplitude of an oscillation, and regulate electrical coupling and synchrony within the olivary network 42, 46, 47. Excitatory afferents and inhibitory cerebellar terminals frequently converge upon the same electrically coupled dendritic spines within the glomerulus, placing their interaction close to the gap junctions that coordinate neighboring neurons. The olive’s output depends steeply on the relative interval between the two inputs. Excitation delivered shortly after inhibition–approximately 50-70 ms later, near the trough of the inhibitory response–generates almost no spikes, whereas excitation delivered approximately 150 ms later, around one oscillatory cycle and near the rebound peak, drives spiking optimally and can evoke more spikes than excitation alone. The same inhibitory input can therefore suppress or facilitate the ensuing climbing-fiber discharge depending on its timing relative to excitation, the phase of the olivary state, and the neuron’s membrane potential 46.

Inhibition also modulates electrical coupling between olivary neurons and can disrupt or reorganize coherent subthreshold oscillations. The cerebellar feedback carrying the prediction may therefore regulate not only whether an incoming error-related excitation produces climbing-fiber spikes, but also the size and synchrony of the olivary ensemble recruited by it—and hence how broadly and synchronously the resulting error signal is delivered across the corresponding Purkinje-cell population 42, 47, 46.

Two qualified conclusions follow. First, cancellation, temporal gating, and ensemble coordination are not cleanly separable stages linked only by anatomy: they are implemented through overlapping interactions among inhibitory input, excitatory input, intrinsic rebound conductances, and electrical coupling in and around the glomerulus. Second, "subtraction" is best understood as a computational description of the closed loop’s net effect, not as literal instantaneous arithmetic performed by an olivary neuron. The proposed biophysical implementation is a state-dependent gate over membrane potential, oscillatory phase, spike probability, and network coupling. Describing that gate as the mechanism of prediction-error subtraction is therefore a plausible synthesis of the evidence, rather than a directly demonstrated identity 42, 46, 45.

Two loose ends complete the picture. The first is why an error signal of this form produces the right synaptic change. Because a given microzone’s climbing fibers are tuned to a particular error direction, an error in that direction drives complex spikes selectively in the cells that control the opposing correction; those complex spikes depress the parallel-fiber synapses that were active just before the error, weakening the simple-spike drive that produced the errant command; and because the microzone’s error tuning is anatomically aligned with the correction it exerts through the nuclei, the net change opposes the error and shrinks it on the following trial 1, 4. It should be said that the parallel-fiber synapse is not the only site the teaching signal reaches: the same climbing-fiber activity instructs plasticity at molecular-layer interneurons and, via the Purkinje-cell output, at the cerebellar nuclei themselves, where learning is consolidated — so the error signal should not be over-located in the cortex. The second loose end is what defines "error" for a given module in the first place. The inferior olive integrates excitatory drive from its own afferents — sensory information relayed directly from spino-olivary and trigeminal pathways from the lower brainstem, and higher-order signals relayed through the mesodiencephalic junction from cortex, superior colliculus, and red nucleus — against the nucleo-olivary inhibition, so the content of the teaching signal is set by which error-reporting inputs a given olivary subregion happens to receive 42, 46, 48. The experiment varies the timing of sensory stimulation (Figure) 76. Complex-spike probability varies with stimulus interval (Figure).

The temporal precision of the error pathway does not arise from a single clock; it is assembled in stages. Intrinsic membrane dynamics constrain when olivary neurons are most excitable; electrical coupling aligns the firing of neurons belonging to the same functional ensemble; the olivocerebellar axons preserve that alignment despite unequal path lengths; and the exceptionally powerful climbing-fiber synapse converts each arriving olivary spike into a sharply defined Purkinje-cell event. These mechanisms solve different timing problems. Subthreshold oscillations provide a phase-dependent temporal framework on the scale of tens to hundreds of milliseconds, whereas electrical coupling, matched conduction times, and climbing-fiber transmission preserve relative timing on the scale of milliseconds or less.

The best-established source of millisecond-scale population precision is regulated electrical coupling within the inferior olive. Olivary neurons are joined dendrite-to-dendrite by connexin36-containing gap junctions concentrated within the glomeruli. These junctions transmit subthreshold voltage fluctuations between neighboring cells, allowing functionally related neurons to approach threshold together. At the cerebellar cortex, the consequence is visible as complex spikes whose onsets are synchronized to within approximately one millisecond, principally among Purkinje cells arranged in the same parasagittal strip 49, 50. Optical recordings reveal the same organization at finer spatial scale: climbing-fiber events coactivate narrow microbands of neighboring Purkinje-cell dendrites, commonly tens of micrometres wide, with correlations consistent with synchrony on a timescale of at most a few milliseconds 51. The study measures complex-spike synchrony (Figure). A 2026 experiment images complex spikes across Purkinje dendrites (Figure).

The causal evidence for this mechanism is unusually strong. Pharmacological reduction of coupling inside the olive decreases both complex-spike synchrony and the associated rhythmic organization 52, while connexin36 deletion reduces olivary electrical coupling and leaves complex-spike synchrony near chance levels without its normal parasagittal distribution 53. The behavioral consequence is not necessarily gross ataxia, but a loss of precision when a movement must be learned at a particular time: connexin36-deficient mice show more variable olivary response latencies and poorly timed conditioned locomotor and eyeblink responses 54. During natural movement, moreover, synchrony is not fixed. It increases and spreads across selected microzones during sharply bounded components of locomotion, whereas the same Purkinje-cell populations are less strongly synchronized at rest 55. The functionally relevant mechanism is therefore not indiscriminately high coupling, but coupling strong enough to form temporally coherent ensembles and sufficiently regulated to recruit only the microzones appropriate to the current event.

Electrical coupling aligns an ensemble, but the temporal state being aligned is supplied partly by the olive’s intrinsic subthreshold membrane-potential oscillations. Olivary neurons possess voltage-dependent conductances that can generate approximately sinusoidal fluctuations in membrane potential 56. In vivo recordings reveal heterogeneous oscillatory regimes: some neurons express faster oscillations in the several-hertz range, others slower low-threshold calcium oscillations, and oscillatory activity may occur in transient epochs rather than continuously 57. When fast oscillations are present, olivary spikes occur preferentially near the depolarized phase, so an input arriving at different points in the cycle does not have an equal probability of producing an immediate climbing-fiber discharge 58. Synaptic inputs and spikes can also reset the phase of the oscillation, allowing an unexpected event to reorganize the timing of subsequent olivary excitability 59.

It is therefore reasonable to describe the oscillation as a temporal scaffold, but not as a universal metronome that assigns every error to a rigid ten-hertz grid. Olivary oscillations are heterogeneous and state-dependent, and rhythmicity can persist in individual neurons after connexin36-dependent coupling has been removed 60, 61, 53. What coupling supplies is principally coherence: uncoupled cells may continue to oscillate at similar frequencies, but their phases and spikes are no longer coordinated across the population. The precision of the teaching signal consequently emerges from the interaction of two properties—intrinsic conductances that create preferred firing phases and gap junctions that align those phases within a temporarily assembled ensemble.

Synchrony generated in the olive would nevertheless be lost if unequal axonal distances converted simultaneous olivary spikes into dispersed cortical arrivals. The olivocerebellar pathway appears to solve this problem through approximate isochrony. In the rat, stimulation near the inferior olive produced complex spikes across widely separated cortical regions after a remarkably uniform conduction time of 3.98±0.363.98 \pm 0.36 ms, despite substantial differences in measured climbing-fiber length 62; longer fibers conducted faster than shorter fibers, thereby compensating for their additional distance. Developmental and dysmyelination experiments further indicate that differential myelination is a major contributor to this compensation: as normal fibers myelinate, the initially larger latency differences across cerebellar regions converge toward a common value, whereas those differences persist in myelin-deficient animals and are accompanied by reduced complex-spike synchrony 63.

Strict isochrony should, however, not be treated as a settled universal property of every olivocerebellar projection. Experiments in the cat 64 and measurements using the climbing-fiber reflex in the rat vermis 65 have reported systematic regional latency differences, although the interpretation of the reflex measurements—and whether they isolate one-way olivocerebellar conduction—has been disputed 66. The defensible conclusion is therefore narrower: compensatory tuning of conduction velocity is strongly supported in the rat pathways examined directly and provides a plausible means of preserving cortical synchrony, but the degree of compensation may vary across species, cerebellar territories, developmental stages, and measurement paradigms.

The final stage is the climbing-fiber–Purkinje-cell synapse, which functions as a high-fidelity temporal relay. A mature Purkinje cell is ordinarily dominated by one climbing fiber whose arbor forms hundreds of release sites over the proximal dendritic tree 67. Release probability is high, several vesicles can be released simultaneously at an individual site, and the resulting compound excitatory conductance is sufficiently large to trigger a complex spike from a single presynaptic olivary action potential 67, 68, 69. The Purkinje cell therefore does not estimate the timing of an error by slowly integrating many weak afferents: the arrival of one climbing-fiber spike produces a rapid, unitary event with little opportunity for probabilistic transmission failure to blur its onset.

Here again, "all-or-none" applies most cleanly to the occurrence and onset of the climbing-fiber response, not to every dimension of the resulting waveform. Complex-spike duration, dendritic calcium entry, and spikelet number vary with olivary burst structure and the state of the Purkinje cell, allowing the same temporally discrete event to carry graded information about teaching strength 36, 70. Nor do all later spikelets necessarily propagate faithfully down the Purkinje-cell axon 71. These qualifications do not undermine the timing mechanism: they separate a relatively reliable event boundary—an olivary spike arrived now—from a graded internal waveform that can determine how strongly that event modifies the circuit.

The loop’s precision is therefore hierarchical rather than unitary. Oscillatory membrane dynamics define preferred temporal windows and permit phase resetting; connexin36-mediated coupling coordinates the particular olivary cells that should report the event; approximate isochrony prevents unequal axonal distances from dispersing their output; and the climbing-fiber synapse converts each arrival into a reliable, sharply initiated complex spike. A climbing fiber may fire only about once per second on average, but low rate is not the same as low temporal resolution: each sparse event can be positioned with millisecond-scale precision relative to the other members of its microzone and embedded within a slower, state-dependent phase structure. In a 2026 human fMRI study, participants learned visual transition regularities without an explicit learning task (Figure) 73. Cerebellar responses tracked incremental prediction errors even though participants made no decisions about the visual sequences (Figure).
